cards.front: What three things does a Claude Project hold together?
cards.back: **Project instructions** (how Claude should behave), **project knowledge** (files Claude should reference) and the project's own **chats**.

cards.front: When should you build a Project instead of using an ordinary chat?
cards.back: When you will reuse the same context, files or rules across many chats, for example a weekly newsletter that must always follow the brand guide.

cards.front: Can Claude read a project's name and description as instructions?
cards.back: No. They help people find and understand the project. Put rules in the **project instructions**.

cards.front: Four qualities of good project knowledge?
cards.back: **Relevant**, **current**, **authoritative** and **clearly named**. Remove superseded versions.

cards.front: What happens on paid plans when project knowledge approaches the context limit?
cards.back: Claude automatically switches to a **retrieval (RAG) mode**, searching the knowledge base and pulling in the most relevant parts instead of reading every file in full.

cards.front: Why does a clean, non-contradictory knowledge base matter more in RAG mode?
cards.back: Claude retrieves the passages that look most relevant. Duplicate or stale files can be retrieved instead of the current one.

cards.front: Project sharing permissions on Team and Enterprise?
cards.back: **Can view**: see and use the project's content and chats. **Can edit**: change instructions and knowledge.

cards.front: Who should get 'can edit' on a shared project?
cards.back: Only the people who own its accuracy. Everyone else gets 'can view' and reports issues.

cards.front: Does memory carry between projects?
cards.back: No. Where memory is on, **each project has its own separate memory space**.

cards.front: Fastest way to check a new Project works?
cards.back: Ask a few questions with **known answers**, including one the documents don't cover, and check that the instructions and the right files are used.

cards.front: Uploaded file vs connector: which one is a snapshot?
cards.back: The **uploaded file**. It stays as uploaded until you replace it. A connector reads the live source.

cards.front: What happens to a Google Doc added to a project from Google Drive?
cards.back: It **syncs from Drive**, so you work with the latest version.

cards.front: Upload or connect: an approved policy that changes twice a year?
cards.back: **Upload** the approved version. It's stable and you want exactly that version.

cards.front: Upload or connect: a planning doc the team edits daily?
cards.back: **Connect** (or add as a synced Drive doc). A snapshot would go stale quickly.

cards.front: Can a connector show Claude files the user can't access?
cards.back: No. Claude **inherits the user's existing permissions** in the connected service.

cards.front: On Team/Enterprise, what must happen before a user can use a connector?
cards.back: An **Owner or admin enables it** for the organisation, then **each user authenticates** individually.

cards.front: Three settings an Owner can apply to each connector action?
cards.back: **Always allow**, **Needs approval**, **Blocked**. For example, allow Drive reading but block creating documents.

cards.front: What can the Gmail connector do?
cards.back: Search and read emails, and draft messages. Sending, replying or forwarding happen with approval.

cards.front: Whose terms govern data in a connected service?
cards.back: The connected service's own terms. It processes data on its own infrastructure, so connect only organisation-approved services.

cards.front: How do you limit which connectors a single chat uses?
cards.back: Toggle connectors on or off per conversation. Enable only what the task needs.

cards.front: Your team needs Claude to reach an internal system with no connector. Associate's move?
cards.back: Hand it to a **Developer or Architect**. Custom connectors are built on remote **MCP** servers.

cards.front: What protocol underlies many connectors, including custom ones?
cards.back: The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**, an open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data.

cards.front: Account-wide vs project instructions vs Skills: scope of each?
cards.back: **Account-wide**: all your chats. **Project**: only chats in that project. **Skills**: packaged instructions and resources Claude loads when relevant.

cards.front: Where does 'use UK spelling' belong if you always want it?
cards.back: **Account-wide instructions**, because it's true for every chat.

cards.front: Seven parts of a strong instruction set?
cards.back: Role/purpose, audience, tone, output format, how to use the knowledge, **what to do when information is missing**, hard rules.

cards.front: Most commonly forgotten instruction that prevents invented answers?
cards.back: What to do when the documents don't cover the question, for example: 'say so and refer to the policy team; do not guess'.

cards.front: Why is 'be accurate and don't make mistakes' a weak instruction?
cards.back: Claude can't act on it. Give specific, checkable directions (sources to use, format, what to do when unsure).

cards.front: Outputs flip between bullets and prose. Likely cause?
cards.back: **Conflicting instructions**, often across layers (account-wide says bullets, project says prose). Resolve the conflict.

cards.front: Should you paste the style guide into instructions as well as uploading it?
cards.back: No. **Point to the file** ('follow the Brand Voice Guide'). Duplication means two copies to maintain.

cards.front: Is memory a good way to enforce a rule?
cards.back: No. Memory is what Claude learns from past chats. **Write rules into instructions.**

cards.front: Do standing instructions guarantee behaviour?
cards.back: No. They make it much more likely. High-stakes output still needs **human review**.

cards.front: Why is stale knowledge dangerous?
cards.back: Claude answers from it **just as confidently** as from current knowledge, with no warning.

cards.front: The configuration maintenance loop?
cards.back: **Inform → Monitor → Update → Verify**, repeated on a schedule and when triggers fire.

cards.front: New price list uploaded, old one kept. Problem?
cards.back: Two conflicting sources. **Replace, don't append**: remove the superseded file.

cards.front: Patch instruction vs removing the stale file: which is the root-cause fix?
cards.back: **Remove or replace the stale file.** A patch instruction fixes one symptom and adds another copy of a fact to maintain.

cards.front: What is a benchmark set for a Project?
cards.back: Five to ten questions with known answers (including a 'not covered' case), run **before and after** every change.

cards.front: Why change one thing at a time?
cards.back: So you can tell which change helped or caused a side effect.

cards.front: What goes in a configuration change log?
cards.back: Date, what changed, **why**, and who changed it.

cards.front: Triggers for reviewing a Project?
cards.back: Source document changes, user reports of wrong answers, audience or purpose changes, connector changes, AI policy changes.

cards.front: A shared helper gave wrong contract answers for weeks. Besides fixing it?
cards.back: **Inform users** what changed and that earlier answers may have been wrong, especially for high-impact topics.
